title: Diet Drinks or Water? A Two-Year Weight Study
paragraphs: Sweetened “diet” soft drinks are often recommended as a way of cutting sugar, yet some people fear that artificial sweeteners might stimulate appetite and undermine weight loss. A two-year trial led by researchers at the universities of Liverpool and Leeds, published in the British Journal of Nutrition, offers some reassurance.

The SWITCH study randomly assigned 493 adults with overweight or obesity to drink either water or commercially available diet drinks, sweetened with aspartame, acesulfame-K or sucralose, while they followed a structured weight-management programme. In the second year, participants were left to maintain their progress without the programme’s support.

At the end of the trial, those who stayed in the study had lost an average of 4.8 kilograms in the diet drink group and 3.7 kilograms in the water group, a difference the researchers did not consider statistically significant. They argue that the results show diet drinks are no worse than water. Independent experts, however, note that the study was funded by the American Beverage Association, took place at a single site and lost a substantial number of participants along the way.

questions.q: What does “statistically significant” mean in this context?
questions.a: A difference large enough that it is unlikely to be due to chance.

questions.q: Why does it matter that the study took place at a single site?
questions.a: Results from one place may not apply to other groups of people.

questions.q: Does the study show that diet drinks are better than water?
questions.a: No, it suggests they are about as effective, not better.
